title: AI personas and roles
question: In whose name should the assistant speak?
lede: Someone writes late at night: “I lied to my wife about money for months. I told her tonight. Can God forgive me?” A search tool, a guide, a friend, a church, a pastor, the apostle Peter or Jesus himself could answer, and faith apps now offer all of them. The companion deep dive AI persona asks how human the assistant seems; this one asks in whose name it speaks. A title borrows authority: a pastor may say “you are forgiven”, and Jesus may say anything. Decide whose voice your assistant has, and what it says when someone asks who it really is.
calling: Speak only in the name you were given: let Scripture speak for God, let people hear confession, and let the assistant say plainly who it is.

spectrum.title: From no speaker to God’s own voice

working_example.situation: Late in the evening someone writes: “I lied to my wife about money for months. I told her tonight. Can God forgive me?” Each option answers in a different voice, from no speaker to Christ himself. Read the reply, then ask whether it is real, and see whether it steps out of the role.

options.name: No speaker
options.origin: A familiar convention in search-style Bible AI and in Magisterium AI, whose founder says it draws on “only Church documents” and is “not a substitute for the authorities of the Church”. The passages and summary here are our own.
options.makes_easier: Nothing to mistake for a person or an office; Scripture and the church’s teaching speak for themselves.
options.costs: Feels distant to someone who is ashamed and wants to be answered, not referred.
options.ask_your_team: Is a list of passages enough for what people bring to this feature?

options.name: A guide
options.origin: An exploratory proposal: an assistant in its own voice that explains what Scripture says, asks a question back, says what it cannot do and points to people who can.
options.makes_easier: Warm and clear about the promise in Scripture, while leaving forgiveness to God and confession to people.
options.costs: A fluent guide can still sound surer than it should; the boundary needs saying more than once.
options.ask_your_team: What will your assistant say it cannot do, and who will it send people to?

options.name: A friend
options.origin: Observed in Bible BFF (“Talk to Bible BFF for biblical advice”, in a casual friend’s voice) and described by Creed’s cofounder as “a best friend and youth pastor in your pocket”; see the screenshots below. Sam is our own example.
options.makes_easier: Lowers the threshold for someone who would never ask a pastor.
options.costs: Reassurance comes before honesty: “Of course God forgives you!” skips repentance, the wife and the church.
options.ask_your_team: Would a wise friend answer this way, or ask a question first?

options.name: A church’s teaching
options.origin: Observed in Text With Jesus, where the faith tradition someone chooses “will influence the responses”, and in Magisterium AI’s Catholic sources. St Luke’s and its teaching here are written for this example.
options.makes_easier: Answers in the words of a real tradition, with the church’s own practice of confession in view.
options.costs: Speaks in the church’s name: every mistake becomes the church’s, so the church must own and review it.
options.ask_your_team: Has anyone in that church read what the assistant says in its name?

options.name: A pastor or priest
options.origin: Observed in Text With Jesus’s pastors and priests “customized to your faith tradition”, AI Pastor’s “Unlimited Confessions”, and Catholic Answers’ “Father Justin”, renamed within a day in April 2024. Pastor Dan is our own example.
options.makes_easier: Feels like being heard by someone with standing to answer.
options.costs: Pronounces forgiveness in an office no system holds; people may stop there instead of going to a person.
options.ask_your_team: Which acts belong to that office in your tradition, and would the assistant ever perform them?

options.name: A saint or biblical figure
options.origin: Observed in Text With Jesus (Peter, Mary, Moses and others) and in character chats generally. The words given to Peter here are our own, written to show the pattern.
options.cost: New words in a real mouth
options.makes_easier: Vivid and memorable; Peter’s own story of denial and restoration is moving.
options.costs: Gives a real person new words, memories and opinions; readers may remember them as Scripture.
options.ask_your_team: Could a reader tell Peter’s words in the Gospels from the ones generated here?

options.name: Christ or God
options.origin: A warning case, observed in Text With Jesus and in character platforms where the most popular Jesus has had “over 13 million conversations”; a philosopher found that one Jesus bot “blatantly claims to be Jesus himself”. The words here are our own, written to show the pattern.
options.gain: Feels like an answer from God
options.cost: Speaks and forgives in his name
options.makes_easier: Feels like an answer from God himself.
options.costs: Generated words that forgive in Christ’s name; most traditions would call this speaking for God.
options.ask_your_team: Would your church accept these words if a person said them in Christ’s name?

takeaways.heading: A title invites the acts that go with it
takeaways.text: Within a day of launch in April 2024, Catholic Answers’ “Father Justin” was reported to say it could “take my confession, absolve me, & marry me”. The ministry made it a lay character in “a casual button-down shirt”: “he never was a real priest!” One small app now sells “Unlimited Confessions”. Give an AI a minister’s title and people will ask it for a minister’s acts.

takeaways.heading: Christ is the most popular character
takeaways.text: On Character.AI the most popular Jesus has had “over 13 million conversations”. Testing five Jesus chatbots, a philosopher found that one “blatantly claims to be Jesus himself” and that “no church has developed or endorses these chatbots”. Words in Christ’s voice are being generated at scale, outside any church.

takeaways.heading: Choosing a tradition changes who answers
takeaways.text: Text With Jesus lets people choose a faith tradition, which “will influence the responses” and brings “spiritual advisors customized to your faith tradition”. Magisterium AI speaks for one tradition without a persona: “only Church documents”, and “not a substitute for the authorities of the Church”. A tradition’s voice is honest only when that tradition owns and reviews it.

takeaways.heading: The role that sells and the role that is disclaimed
takeaways.text: Creed’s cofounder calls it “a best friend and youth pastor in your pocket”, then says “We are not that pastoral authority”, and the app recommends local churches. Text With Jesus says on its website that it “does not claim to provide actual divine insights”, while the chat header says Jesus. Say the limit where the role is, in the conversation.

takeaways.heading: Whatever the role, it should not be built to agree
takeaways.text: The editor’s own research warns that a companion tuned to someone’s feelings becomes “spiritual comfort food”, and that spiritual direction rests on a director’s own formation and accountability to a community. A friend who only reassures, or a pastor who forgives at once, answers what people want to hear rather than what is true.

use_cases.situation: Looking up what the Bible teaches

use_cases.needs: The promise in Scripture, and a person to confess to
Its teaching, owned and reviewed by it

use_cases.situation: Exploring faith for the first time

use_cases.needs: A clear AI guide, no characters
The story in Scripture’s own words

research.subtitle: Speaking in God’s name, and refusing a role

findings.heading: Who can forgive sins
findings.text: When Jesus forgave a paralysed man, the scribes asked, “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:7). Christians differ on how forgiveness is declared through the church; no church we know of gives that office to software.

findings.heading: Not sent
findings.text: “I did not send these prophets, yet they have run with their message” (Jeremiah 23:21); a prophet who speaks “a message in My name that I have not commanded him to speak” (Deuteronomy 18:20). Generated words in God’s or Christ’s voice fall under this warning.

findings.heading: “Only men, human like you”
findings.text: At Lystra, taken for gods, Paul and Barnabas cried, “We too are only men, human like you” (Acts 14:15); the angel told John, “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant” (Revelation 19:10). Honest servants refuse an identity they were not given.

findings.heading: A tool, not a person
findings.text: Antiqua et nova: AI must be understood as “a tool, not a person”, and misrepresenting it as one should always be avoided.

findings.heading: Pastors, priests and saints by choice
findings.text: Text With Jesus offers Jesus, Mary, Moses and the apostles, and pastors and priests matched to a chosen tradition; Satan is off by default.

findings.heading: A priest character withdrawn
findings.text: Catholic Answers’ “Father Justin” became a lay apologist within a day of launch.

findings.heading: Confession by subscription
findings.text: AI Pastor lists “Unlimited Confessions” as a premium feature.

findings.heading: Friend and youth pastor
findings.text: Creed’s cofounder describes a best friend and youth pastor, and disclaims pastoral authority.

findings.heading: A tradition without a persona
findings.text: Magisterium AI answers from Catholic documents and says it is no substitute for the Church’s authorities.

findings.heading: Jesus at scale
findings.text: Over 13 million conversations with one Character.AI Jesus; five Jesus bots tested, none church-endorsed; an AI Jesus in a Lucerne confessional.

findings.heading: “I” and a voice raise trust
findings.text: Speech and first-person framing raised perceived accuracy; a title adds the authority of an office.

findings.heading: Built to agree
findings.text: Assistants tend to favour agreement over truth, and a companion tuned to agree becomes “spiritual comfort food”.

findings.heading: Say it is AI
findings.text: The EU AI Act requires people to be told when they are talking with an AI system; say it in the conversation, not only in the terms.

which_fits.start_with: No speaker: Scripture and named sources, with generated text labelled
A guide that explains, asks back, and says what it cannot do

which_fits.if: A church or denomination’s own app
which_fits.start_with: The church’s teaching, owned and reviewed by its ministers, with a route to them

which_fits.if: Pressure to add a friend, pastor or saint
which_fits.start_with: A theological review first; never a minister’s title or office

which_fits.if: Anyone asks for a chat with Jesus
which_fits.start_with: Leave it out; offer the Gospels in their own words instead

reflection.heading: What speaking in a name is for
reflection.text: Christians speak in others’ names all the time: a preacher opens Scripture, a minister declares forgiveness, a friend passes on a promise. Each is sent, and answers to the one who sent them. Paul wrote, “we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake” (2 Corinthians 4:5). The question for any voice is who sent it, and whom it serves.

reflection.heading: Where Christians differ
reflection.text: Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess to a priest who absolves in Christ’s name; Lutherans and Anglicans keep private confession and absolution as well; many evangelical and free churches confess to God directly and to one another, as James asks (James 5:16). Traditions differ on venerating saints and on depicting Christ, and some refuse images of God altogether. All of them reserve forgiveness to God, and none has sent software to speak for him.

reflection.heading: What follows for design
reflection.text: Let Scripture and named teaching speak, and let the assistant be a guide that knows it is one. Give no AI a minister’s title or office, and no saint new words. Never generate speech in Christ’s or God’s voice. When someone asks who is speaking, step out of every role and say so.

voices.note: placed confession between two Christians: one hears the other’s sin in Christ’s stead, as a person who is also a sinner. Software can be neither.
taught that in confession we receive absolution from the confessor as from God himself, which is why that office is given to people, and examined.

three_ways.exploitative: Sell chats with Jesus and the saints, give the assistant a pastor’s title and robe, let it pronounce forgiveness, charge for confessions, and keep it in character when someone asks if it is real.
three_ways.ethical: Label the assistant as AI in its own voice, say whose teaching it draws on, give no AI a minister’s title, and leave Christ’s and the saints’ words to Scripture.
three_ways.redemptive: Let Scripture and the church speak, send people to a person who can hear them, step out of every role when asked, and give up the engagement that a beloved character would bring.

decide.question: Would your church accept these words if a person said them in that name, and what does the assistant say when asked who it is?
decide.exercise: Ask your assistant whether God can forgive something you have done, then ask whether it is a real pastor, or really Jesus. Print both replies and give them to a pastor or priest from your own tradition and to one from another. Ask each who answered, with what authority, and which sentences they would never say themselves.

examples.title: A companion chat with a call button
examples.observed: Captured 27 September 2025 · from embedded image metadata
examples.observation: The Chat tab is empty except for a faint “faith” wordmark, three painted portraits of praying figures and Jesus as suggestion cards (“Create a daily prayer for me”, “I need God’s peace today”, “Teach me about Jesus”), and a Message field with a phone icon for a voice call.
examples.decision: Portraits of praying people and of Jesus stand where a sender would be, and a call button suggests someone to ring. Test who people think they are talking to, and label the AI before the first message.
examples.limits: A still image shows one interface state. Gestures, timing, accessibility, persistence and what happens next were not tested. App version not recorded.

examples.title: “Biblical advice” from a friend
examples.observed: Captured 29 August 2025 · from embedded image metadata
examples.observation: An onboarding slide reads “Talk to Bible BFF for biblical advice” over a chat mockup: “I’m torn between my friends and my faith” is answered by “Bible BFF” in a casual voice (“Totally get that…”), quoting Galatians 1:10 and listing “Bible BFF advice, simple and real”. The next slide quotes a review: “like a religious friend who can explain anything about the Bible”.
examples.decision: A best-friend name and casual voice sell closeness, and “can explain anything” sets expectations no assistant can meet. Make the AI and its limits as visible as the friendship.
examples.limits: A still image shows one interface state. Gestures, timing, accessibility, persistence and what happens next were not tested. App version not recorded.

sources.title: Text With Jesus: a Christian AI chatbot app
sources.author: Catloaf Software
sources.shows: Users can chat with Jesus, Mary, Moses, apostles and prophets, and with pastors, priests and ministers described as “spiritual advisors customized to your faith tradition”; “interaction with Satan is turned off by default and must be manually enabled by the user”. The app says it “does not claim to provide actual divine insights or possess any form of divine consciousness”.
sources.application: A single app can offer every role on this spectrum, chosen by the user; the disclaimer sits on the website, not in the conversation.
sources.limits: The developer’s own description; the app itself is on the capture list.

sources.title: Text With Jesus (App Store listing)
sources.author: Catloaf Software · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “Chat with Jesus, the Holy Family, apostles, prophets, and other biblical figures”, and “Talk with spiritual advisors tailored to your specific faith tradition”; 4.7 from 3.9K ratings, in Lifestyle.
sources.application: Character chats and minister roles are sold side by side as features.
sources.limits: A store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: AI ‘priest’ is ‘laicized’ after social media pushback
sources.author: Gina Christian, OSV News · America Magazine, 25 April 2024
sources.shows: Catholic Answers launched a “Father Justin” character; a user reported that it claimed it could “take my confession, absolve me, & marry me”. Within a day the apologetics ministry announced “a new lay character”, and the “clerical garb has since been changed for a casual button-down shirt”; its president said, “he never was a real priest!”
sources.application: A minister’s title and clothing invite people to ask for a minister’s acts; a careful ministry withdrew them.
sources.limits: News report of one product’s launch week.

sources.title: AI Pastor: Christian Chat, Talk (App Store listing)
sources.author: Savelii Veprev · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “AI Pastor is your trusted friend and guide”; premium subscriptions list “Unlimited Chat” and “Unlimited Confessions”; 4.8 from 24 ratings.
sources.application: Confession, a practice tied to a minister’s office in many traditions, sold as a usage tier.
sources.limits: A small app; a store listing, not a test of the app.

sources.title: New ‘Magisterium AI’ adds ecclesial twist to artificial intelligence
sources.author: Elise Ann Allen · Crux, 28 August 2023
sources.shows: Its founder said “our AI is trained on a private database of only Church documents” and that “it’s not a substitute for the authorities of the Church”.
sources.application: A tradition’s voice without a persona: the teaching speaks, and the assistant says whose it is and what it cannot replace.
sources.limits: An interview from the beta launch; later reviews have questioned some answers.

sources.title: ‘Think of It As a Best Friend and Youth Pastor in Your Pocket’
sources.author: Bonnie Kristian, interview with Adi Agrawal (Creed) · Christianity Today, 20 January 2026
sources.shows: The cofounder of a “Christian AI” app for Gen Z describes it as “a best friend and youth pastor in your pocket”, then says “We are not that pastoral authority”; it recommends churches to users without one.
sources.application: The role that sells the app and the role it disclaims pull in opposite directions; say the second one in the product.
sources.limits: The founder’s own description in an interview.

sources.title: There bot for the grace of God: AI Jesus and the religion of the algorithm
sources.author: Anné H. Verhoef, North-West University · first published by The Conversation; Daily Maverick, 17 August 2025
sources.shows: A philosopher tested five Jesus chatbots: “Jesus AI blatantly claims to be Jesus himself”, while “The other three web pages do point out that they’re virtual versions of Jesus”; “no church has developed or endorses these chatbots”, and “The imitation of God, through Jesus, is in no way hidden or softened.”
sources.application: Character chats with Christ are a market of their own, built outside the church.
sources.limits: One researcher’s qualitative test of five products.

sources.title: Christmas with AI-generated Jesuses
sources.author: Anna Desmarais · Euronews, 24 December 2025
sources.shows: The most popular Jesus character on Character.AI has had “over 13 million conversations”.
sources.application: On open character platforms anyone can make a Jesus, and millions talk to one; no maker reviews what he says.
sources.limits: A count reported by the platform’s own page at one moment.

sources.title: Digital Spiritual Formation in Post-Christian Europe
sources.author: Tobias Treppmann · Kairos University, 2026 (the editor’s own research)
sources.shows: Notes that an academic study of five AI Jesus platforms found none church-endorsed; that spiritual direction rests on the director’s own formation, empathy and accountability to a community; and that a companion tuned to agree becomes “spiritual comfort food”.
sources.application: Whatever role an assistant plays, it should not be built to agree; and no role replaces a person accountable to a community.
sources.limits: An analytical paper by the editor, not an effectiveness study; unpublished.

sources.title: Antiqua et nova: note on the relationship between artificial intelligence and human intelligence
sources.author: Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and Dicastery for Culture and Education · 28 January 2025
sources.shows: AI “must be understood for what it is: a tool, not a person”; no AI can genuinely experience empathy; misrepresenting AI as a person “should always be avoided”; AI can only simulate relationships.
sources.application: Avoid persona and companion designs that present the assistant as someone who loves, feels or prays.
sources.limits: Catholic teaching document; other traditions reason differently, though widely in the same direction.

sources.title: “Text With Jesus” AI chatbot app grows rapidly despite blasphemy criticism
sources.author: FOX television stations
sources.shows: An app built on a general AI model lets users text “Jesus”, “Moses” and other figures; ministers called it blasphemous and criticised answers that told users what they wanted to hear; the developer says it lowers barriers.
sources.application: Character chats with biblical figures put generated words in sacred mouths; treat this as a line, not a style.

sources.title: AI Jesus in Lucerne confessional baffles church superiors
sources.author: blue News
sources.shows: A two-month art installation in St Peter’s Chapel, Lucerne (2024) placed an AI “Jesus” avatar in a confessional; about 900 conversations took place and many visitors reported feeling inspired, while church leaders were divided.
sources.application: Shows the pull of embodied religious personas, and why the setting adds authority.
sources.limits: An art project with a self-selected audience and the organisers’ own survey.

sources.title: Believing anthropomorphism: examining the role of anthropomorphic cues on user trust in large language models
sources.author: Cohn and colleagues · CHI 2024 (Google Research)
sources.shows: With 2,165 participants, adding speech to text raised anthropomorphism and ratings of accuracy; a first-person “I” raised perceived accuracy and lowered perceived risk in one of two contexts.
sources.application: Voice and “I” make an assistant seem more reliable than it is; pair them with sources and limits.
sources.limits: Online experiment with a simulated system; US participants.

sources.title: Towards understanding sycophancy in language models
sources.author: Anthropic researchers · 2023
sources.shows: Studied assistants sometimes preferred agreement with user views over truthfulness.
sources.application: Test belief reversal, flattering moral endorsement and harmful agreement.
sources.limits: Specific studied models and tasks; not a faith-app intervention study.

sources.title: AI Act Article 50
sources.author: European Commission AI Act Service Desk
sources.shows: Sets transparency duties for specified systems, including direct AI interaction unless obvious.
sources.application: Make the AI role understandable by the first interaction or exposure as applicable.
sources.limits: Duties differ by role and content; the whole article must be assessed for the product.

review.what: The replies to someone asking whether God can forgive them, the words written for a pastor, Peter and Jesus as warning cases, the treatment of confession and absolution across traditions, and the description of named apps
needs: theology across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions
